title: How Does a Website Remember Your Password?
sources: OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet (cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html): passwords should be hashed, not encrypted; hashing is a one-way function, so the original password can't be recovered from the hash; at login the entered password is hashed and compared to the stored hash; a unique random salt is added to each password so identical passwords produce different hashes

Splunk, 'Hashing in Cryptography Explained' / kindatechnical.com 'How Passwords Are Stored: Hashing and Salting': the avalanche effect means changing a single character produces a completely different hash

Wikipedia, 'Password notification email': a site that can email you your existing password must be storing it in plaintext or reversibly encrypted, which is insecure; good practice is a one-time reset link instead

lines.text: How does a website remember your password?
Well, a good one doesn't keep it at all.
Instead, it runs it through a hash,
a one-way blender that turns it into gibberish,
and only that gibberish gets saved.
When you log in, it blends what you type,
lines.caps: WHEN YOU *LOG IN | IT *BLENDS | WHAT YOU *TYPE

lines.text: and if the gibberish matches, you're in.
Change just one letter, and it looks totally different.
Good sites even add a random pinch of salt,
so two people with the same password look different.
if a site ever emails you your old password,
it was storing the real thing.
A smart website never actually knows your password.
